Kappa and finite-sample concentration

How much does averaging reduce mean absolute error at a specified sample size? Kappa records the growth of the sum’s absolute deviation between two sizes. It depends on the whole distribution and the chosen sizes. A tail exponent alone does not determine it.

We use the metric from Taleb (2025), ch. 8, §§8.1–8.3, pp. 154–160. The derivations below establish the stated special cases and corrections; simulated values are labeled separately. The chapter guide maps the remaining source sections.

Definition and domain¶

Let XiX_iXi​ be iid, with E∣X1∣<∞\mathbb E|X_1|<\inftyE∣X1​∣<∞, mean μ\muμ, and sums Sn=∑i=1nXiS_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_iSn​=∑i=1n​Xi​, as in the shared notation. Define

M(n)=E∣Sn−nμ∣,A(n)=E∣Xˉn−μ∣=M(n)/n.\begin{aligned} M(n)&=\mathbb E|S_n-n\mu|,\\ A(n)&=\mathbb E|\bar X_n-\mu|\\ &=M(n)/n. \end{aligned}M(n)A(n)​=E∣Sn​−nμ∣,=E∣Xˉn​−μ∣=M(n)/n.​
(1)

MMM is a mean absolute deviation about the population mean, without Gaussian calibration. It is neither a median deviation nor a deviation about an estimated center; see the dispersion note. For integers n>n0≥1n>n_0\ge1n>n0​≥1, with M(n)>M(n0)>0M(n)>M(n_0)>0M(n)>M(n0​)>0, set

κn0,n=2−log⁡(n/n0)log⁡(M(n)/M(n0)),M(n)M(n0)=(n/n0)1/(2−κn0,n).\begin{aligned} \kappa_{n_0,n} &=2-\frac{\log(n/n_0)}{\log(M(n)/M(n_0))},\\ \frac{M(n)}{M(n_0)} &=(n/n_0)^{1/(2-\kappa_{n_0,n})}. \end{aligned}κn0​,n​M(n0​)M(n)​​=2−log(M(n)/M(n0​))log(n/n0​)​,=(n/n0​)1/(2−κn0​,n​).​
(2)

We always print both indices. The source’s κ1\kappa_1κ1​ means κ1,2\kappa_{1,2}κ1,2​, whereas κ1,n\kappa_{1,n}κ1,n​ compares size nnn with one observation. An adjacent-size comparison κn,n+1\kappa_{n,n+1}κn,n+1​ is different. Here “metric” names a concentration index, not a distance satisfying the axioms of a metric space.

We prove three elementary properties. Adding a constant to every summand cancels under centering; multiplying by b≠0b\ne0b=0 multiplies both deviations by ∣b∣|b|∣b∣. Thus kappa is invariant under location and nonzero scale changes. Conditional Jensen, applied to an independent centered increment, gives M(n+1)≥M(n)M(n+1)\ge M(n)M(n+1)≥M(n). The triangle inequality gives M(n)≤nM(1)M(n)\le nM(1)M(n)≤nM(1). Consequently κ1,n≤1\kappa_{1,n}\le1κ1,n​≤1 wherever the displayed definition applies. There is no universal lower bound of zero.

For a chain n0<n1<⋯<nrn_0<n_1<\cdots<n_rn0​<n1​<⋯<nr​, logarithmic growth adds:

log⁡M(nr)M(n0)=∑j=1rlog⁡(nj/nj−1)2−κnj−1,nj.\begin{aligned} &\log\frac{M(n_r)}{M(n_0)}\\ &\quad=\sum_{j=1}^r \frac{\log(n_j/n_{j-1})}{2-\kappa_{n_{j-1},n_j}}. \end{aligned}​logM(n0​)M(nr​)​=j=1∑r​2−κnj−1​,nj​​log(nj​/nj−1​)​.​
(3)

This is a telescoping identity, with each intermediate kappa defined. It does not justify averaging the kappas themselves.

Use kappa_from_mads and stable_kappa to expose the boundaries explicitly:

from xmath.incerto.concentration import kappa_from_mads, stable_kappa

for m0, m in ((1, 2**0.5), (2/3, 14/15), (1, 1), (0, 0), (float("inf"), float("inf"))):
    print(f"MADs {m0:.4g}, {m:.4g}: {kappa_from_mads(m0, m, 2):z.4f}")
for alpha in (1, 1.5, 2):
    print(f"Stable alpha={alpha:g}: {stable_kappa(alpha):.4g}")

Output

MADs 1, 1.414: 0.0000
MADs 0.6667, 0.9333: -0.0600
MADs 1, 1: -inf
MADs 0, 0: nan
MADs inf, inf: nan
Stable alpha=1: nan
Stable alpha=1.5: 0.5
Stable alpha=2: 0

The equal-positive case uses an extended limit. Constant laws and laws without a finite absolute first moment have no kappa under this definition. In particular, a Cauchy law is a limiting benchmark as the stable index decreases to one, not an admissible endpoint.

Stable benchmark and attraction¶

For a nondegenerate stable law of index 1<α≤21<\alpha\le21<α≤2, the centered sum has the same distribution as n1/α(X1−μ)n^{1/\alpha}(X_1-\mu)n1/α(X1​−μ). Taking absolute expectations proves

M(n)=n1/αM(1),κn0,n=2−α,A(n)/M(1)=n1/α−1.\begin{aligned} M(n)&=n^{1/\alpha}M(1),\\ \kappa_{n_0,n}&=2-\alpha,\\ A(n)/M(1)&=n^{1/\alpha-1}. \end{aligned}M(n)κn0​,n​A(n)/M(1)​=n1/αM(1),=2−α,=n1/α−1.​
(4)

The stable sum identity is the cited structural property; the algebraic consequence for kappa is proved here. Skewness does not change the exponent, so it cancels from kappa even though it can change M(1)M(1)M(1). At α=2\alpha=2α=2 the law is Gaussian and kappa is zero. The growth exponent is 1/α1/\alpha1/α; it must not be substituted for α\alphaα in 2−α2-\alpha2−α. The stable-law note fixes the characteristic-function scale and proves the symmetric MAD formula.

A domain-of-attraction statement is weaker than the exact stable identity. For example, suppose a centered sum divided by ana_nan​ converges in law to an integrable stable variable ZZZ, the normalized absolute sums are uniformly integrable, and log⁡an/log⁡n→1/α\log a_n/\log n\to1/\alphalogan​/logn→1/α. Then

M(n)/an⟶E∣Z∣M(n)/a_n\longrightarrow\mathbb E|Z|M(n)/an​⟶E∣Z∣
(5)

and substitution gives κ1,n→2−α\kappa_{1,n}\to2-\alphaκ1,n​→2−α. Uniform integrability is what permits convergence of expectations; weak convergence alone does not supply it. This conditional argument does not assert a finite-sample rate for every regularly varying law. A one-sided Pareto and a symmetric Student law with the same tail exponent can have different finite kappas: both their centers and their distribution bodies differ. The numerical comparison below concerns exponent three only.

Student sums and a logarithmic limit¶

Use the ordinary Student law with degrees of freedom ν>1\nu>1ν>1, location zero and scale one. Locally ν\nuν is also its power-tail exponent. A direct beta integral gives

M(1)=νπ Γ((ν−1)/2)Γ(ν/2).M(1)=\sqrt{\frac\nu\pi}\, \frac{\Gamma((\nu-1)/2)}{\Gamma(\nu/2)}.M(1)=πν​​Γ(ν/2)Γ((ν−1)/2)​.
(6)

For completeness, substitute v=1+x2/νv=1+x^2/\nuv=1+x2/ν in 2∫0∞xfν(x) dx2\int_0^\infty x f_\nu(x)\,dx2∫0∞​xfν​(x)dx; the remaining integral is ∫1∞v−(ν+1)/2 dv=2/(ν−1)\int_1^\infty v^{-(\nu+1)/2}\,dv=2/(\nu-1)∫1∞​v−(ν+1)/2dv=2/(ν−1). The gamma recurrence yields the displayed expression.

There is also a two-summand closed form. Write a=ν/2a=\nu/2a=ν/2 and Xi=ν/(2Gi)ZiX_i=\sqrt{\nu/(2G_i)}Z_iXi​=ν/(2Gi​)​Zi​, where the GiG_iGi​ are independent Gamma(a,1)(a,1)(a,1) and the ZiZ_iZi​ are independent standard normals, independent of the GiG_iGi​. Set T=G1+G2T=G_1+G_2T=G1​+G2​, B=G1/TB=G_1/TB=G1​/T. The change of variables has Jacobian TTT and factorizes the joint density into independent Gamma(2a,1)(2a,1)(2a,1) and Beta(a,a)(a,a)(a,a) densities. Conditional normal absolute moments therefore give

M(2)=ν/π E[T−1/2]×E[(B(1−B))−1/2],M(2)M(1)=π 22−νΓ(ν−1/2)Γ(ν/2)2.\begin{aligned} M(2)&=\sqrt{\nu/\pi}\, \mathbb E[T^{-1/2}]\\ &\quad\times\mathbb E[(B(1-B))^{-1/2}],\\ \frac{M(2)}{M(1)} &=\sqrt\pi\,2^{2-\nu} \frac{\Gamma(\nu-1/2)}{\Gamma(\nu/2)^2}. \end{aligned}M(2)M(1)M(2)​​=ν/π​E[T−1/2]×E[(B(1−B))−1/2],=π​22−νΓ(ν/2)2Γ(ν−1/2)​.​
(7)

The second line follows by the gamma and beta integrals, followed by the gamma duplication identity. These are finite precisely when ν>1\nu>1ν>1.

Cubic Student: every integer size¶

At ν=3\nu=3ν=3, the characteristic function is ϕ(t)=(1+3∣t∣)e−3∣t∣\phi(t)=(1+\sqrt3|t|)e^{-\sqrt3|t|}ϕ(t)=(1+3​∣t∣)e−3​∣t∣. One way to verify it is to differentiate the Cauchy Fourier integral ∫Reitx(x2+a2)−1dx=πe−a∣t∣/a\int_{\mathbb R}e^{itx}(x^2+a^2)^{-1}dx=\pi e^{-a|t|}/a∫R​eitx(x2+a2)−1dx=πe−a∣t∣/a with respect to a>0a>0a>0 and use the normalized squared-denominator density at a=3a=\sqrt3a=3​. The Cauchy integral follows by closing the contour in the half-plane where the exponential decays and taking the residue at iaiaia or −ia-ia−ia; the arc integral tends to zero. Differentiation is justified by an integrable bound in a neighborhood of any positive aaa.

We now derive the sum MAD, using the absolute-moment Fourier identity. Integration by parts, then u=3tu=\sqrt3tu=3​t, gives

In=∫0∞(1+u)n−1e−nu du,M(n)=23π nIn,M(n)M(1)=enn1−nΓ(n,n),Γ(n,n)=∫n∞tn−1e−t dt.\begin{aligned} I_n&=\int_0^\infty(1+u)^{n-1}e^{-nu}\,du,\\ M(n)&=\frac{2\sqrt3}{\pi}\,nI_n,\\ \frac{M(n)}{M(1)} &=e^n n^{1-n}\Gamma(n,n),\\ \Gamma(n,n)&=\int_n^\infty t^{n-1}e^{-t}\,dt. \end{aligned}In​M(n)M(1)M(n)​Γ(n,n)​=∫0∞​(1+u)n−1e−nudu,=π23​​nIn​,=enn1−nΓ(n,n),=∫n∞​tn−1e−tdt.​
(8)

The boundary term vanishes at zero because 1−ϕ(t)n=O(t2)1-\phi(t)^n=O(t^2)1−ϕ(t)n=O(t2), and at infinity because the numerator is bounded. The substitution t=n(1+u)t=n(1+u)t=n(1+u) gives the incomplete-gamma expression. This also holds at n=1n=1n=1. Repeated integration by parts yields the independent finite formula

M(n)M(1)=n!nn∑j=0n−1njj!.\frac{M(n)}{M(1)} =\frac{n!}{n^n}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\frac{n^j}{j!}.M(1)M(n)​=nnn!​j=0∑n−1​j!nj​.
(9)

For the limit, e−n∑j<nnj/j!=P(Nn<n)→1/2e^{-n}\sum_{j<n}n^j/j!=P(N_n<n)\to1/2e−n∑j<n​nj/j!=P(Nn​<n)→1/2, where NnN_nNn​ is Poisson with mean nnn. Apply the classical CLT to a sum of nnn independent Poisson(1)(1)(1) variables. Stirling’s formula then gives

M(n)M(1)∼πn/2,log⁡n  κ1,n⟶2log⁡(π/2).\begin{aligned} \frac{M(n)}{M(1)}&\sim\sqrt{\pi n/2},\\ \log n\;\kappa_{1,n}&\longrightarrow2\log(\pi/2). \end{aligned}M(1)M(n)​lognκ1,n​​∼πn/2​,⟶2log(π/2).​
(10)

This constant differs from the one printed in §8.6.1, p. 165. The calculation concerns the kappa anchored at one observation. It is not a bound on the CDF error in a normal approximation, nor on tail-quantile error. It does not prove that a million-term standardized sum is poorly approximated by a Gaussian at every threshold.

What the logarithmic rate measures¶

More generally, take any iid law with variance 0<σ2<∞0<\sigma^2<\infty0<σ2<∞. The classical CLT is cited in the limit-law note. The normalized centered sums have second moment σ2\sigma^2σ2; hence E[∣Yn∣1∣Yn∣>K]≤σ2/K\mathbb E[|Y_n|\mathbf1_{|Y_n|>K}]\le\sigma^2/KE[∣Yn​∣1∣Yn​∣>K​]≤σ2/K for Yn=(Sn−nμ)/nY_n=(S_n-n\mu)/\sqrt nYn​=(Sn​−nμ)/n​. This proves uniform integrability, so

M(n)/n⟶c,c=σ2/π,log⁡n  κ1,n⟶4log⁡cM(1).\begin{aligned} M(n)/\sqrt n&\longrightarrow c,\\ c&=\sigma\sqrt{2/\pi},\\ \log n\;\kappa_{1,n} &\longrightarrow4\log\frac{c}{M(1)}. \end{aligned}M(n)/n​clognκ1,n​​⟶c,=σ2/π​,⟶4logM(1)c​.​
(11)

To obtain the last line, write log⁡(M(n)/M(1))=12log⁡n+log⁡(c/M(1))+o(1)\log(M(n)/M(1))=\tfrac12\log n+\log(c/M(1))+o(1)log(M(n)/M(1))=21​logn+log(c/M(1))+o(1) and substitute in the definition. The logarithmic behavior can reflect the mismatch between the one-observation MAD and its Gaussian calibration. If c=M(1)c=M(1)c=M(1), the constant vanishes and this argument gives no nonzero leading rate. Kappa approaching zero does not identify the far tail.

Exponential and gamma sums¶

Let each summand have Gamma shape r>0r>0r>0 and scale θ>0\theta>0θ>0. Here θ\thetaθ is a local scale, not a natural parameter. The sum has shape a=nra=nra=nr, mean aθa\thetaaθ, and

M(n)=2θ aae−aΓ(a).M(n)=\frac{2\theta\,a^a e^{-a}}{\Gamma(a)}.M(n)=Γ(a)2θaae−a​.
(12)

We derive this using E∣V−EV∣=2E(V−EV)+\mathbb E|V-\mathbb EV|=2\mathbb E(V-\mathbb EV)_+E∣V−EV∣=2E(V−EV)+​. After scaling by θ\thetaθ, the integral is

2θΓ(a)∫a∞(t−a)ta−1e−t dt.\frac{2\theta}{\Gamma(a)} \int_a^\infty(t-a)t^{a-1}e^{-t}\,dt.Γ(a)2θ​∫a∞​(t−a)ta−1e−tdt.
(13)

Integration by parts gives Γ(a+1,a)=aΓ(a,a)+aae−a\Gamma(a+1,a)=a\Gamma(a,a)+a^ae^{-a}Γ(a+1,a)=aΓ(a,a)+aae−a, which evaluates the integral. At r=1r=1r=1, the parent is exponential with rate 1/θ1/\theta1/θ. Stirling’s formula or the preceding finite-variance argument gives

log⁡n  κ1,n⟶4−2log⁡(2π).\log n\;\kappa_{1,n} \longrightarrow4-2\log(2\pi).lognκ1,n​⟶4−2log(2π).
(14)

Thus even the exponential law has a positive finite kappa and this logarithmic anchored rate. It still satisfies the Cramér condition and is not subexponential.

Use gaussian_sum_mad, student_sum_mad, gamma_sum_mad, and kappa_from_mads.

from xmath.incerto.concentration import (
    gaussian_sum_mad, student_sum_mad, gamma_sum_mad, kappa_from_mads,
)

for name, mad in (("Gaussian", gaussian_sum_mad), ("Student 3", student_sum_mad), ("Exponential", gamma_sum_mad)):
    for n in (2, 32, 1000):
        print(f"{name}, n={n}: kappa={kappa_from_mads(mad(1), mad(n), n):z.3f}")

Lognormal sums¶

Let X=eμℓ+σℓZX=e^{\mu_\ell+\sigma_\ell Z}X=eμℓ​+σℓ​Z with standard-normal ZZZ and σℓ>0\sigma_\ell>0σℓ​>0. These are log-location and log-scale, not the mean and standard deviation of XXX. Write m=EX=eμℓ+σℓ2/2m=\mathbb EX=e^{\mu_\ell+\sigma_\ell^2/2}m=EX=eμℓ​+σℓ2​/2. Completing the square in the truncated normal integral gives

M(1)=2m[2Φ(σℓ/2)−1].M(1)=2m\left[2\Phi(\sigma_\ell/2)-1\right].M(1)=2m[2Φ(σℓ​/2)−1].
(15)

For example, use M(1)=2E(X−m)+M(1)=2\mathbb E(X-m)_+M(1)=2E(X−m)+​ and the threshold Z=σℓ/2Z=\sigma_\ell/2Z=σℓ​/2. Exponential tilting shifts the normal mean by σℓ\sigma_\ellσℓ​, giving the formula. Sums of independent lognormals are not generally lognormal. Matching a sum’s first two moments to another lognormal gives an approximation, not an identity or a proved bound on kappa.

The mismatch can be checked with third moments. For a mean-one lognormal, put v=eσℓ2−1>0v=e^{\sigma_\ell^2}-1>0v=eσℓ2​−1>0. Its moments EVj=ej(j−1)σℓ2/2\mathbb EV^j=e^{j(j-1)\sigma_\ell^2/2}EVj=ej(j−1)σℓ2​/2 give variance vvv and third centered moment v2(v+3)v^2(v+3)v2(v+3). Independence makes the variance of the average v/nv/nv/n and its third centered moment v2(v+3)/n2v^2(v+3)/n^2v2(v+3)/n2. The skewnesses of the actual average and a moment-matched lognormal are therefore

gsum=(v+3)v/n,gfit=(v/n+3)v/n.\begin{aligned} g_{\rm sum}&=(v+3)\sqrt{v/n},\\ g_{\rm fit}&=(v/n+3)\sqrt{v/n}. \end{aligned}gsum​gfit​​=(v+3)v/n​,=(v/n+3)v/n​.​
(16)

They differ for every n>1n>1n>1. This proves that the fitted lognormal cannot be the exact sum law; it does not quantify its approximation error.

We prove the three limits at the scope used in §8.6.2, pp. 166–168. For fixed σℓ\sigma_\ellσℓ​, finite variance and the previous argument give κ1,n→0\kappa_{1,n}\to0κ1,n​→0 as n→∞n\to\inftyn→∞. For fixed integer n>1n>1n>1, scale invariance lets us use the mean-one variable Vσ=eσZ−σ2/2V_\sigma=e^{\sigma Z-\sigma^2/2}Vσ​=eσZ−σ2/2. Define its Gaussian approximation error DσD_\sigmaDσ​. As σ↓0\sigma\downarrow0σ↓0,

Dσ=Vσ−1σ−Z,EDσ2=eσ2−1σ2−1⟶0.\begin{aligned} D_\sigma&=\frac{V_\sigma-1}{\sigma}-Z,\\ \mathbb E D_\sigma^2&=\frac{e^{\sigma^2}-1}{\sigma^2}-1\\ &\longrightarrow0. \end{aligned}Dσ​EDσ2​​=σVσ​−1​−Z,=σ2eσ2−1​−1⟶0.​
(17)

This identity follows from EVσ2=eσ2\mathbb E V_\sigma^2=e^{\sigma^2}EVσ2​=eσ2 and E[ZVσ]=σ\mathbb E[ZV_\sigma]=\sigmaE[ZVσ​]=σ. A finite sum preserves L2L^2L2 convergence, which implies convergence of absolute expectations. Thus the MAD ratio tends to n\sqrt nn​, and kappa tends to zero.

As σ→∞\sigma\to\inftyσ→∞, couple a fixed finite set of normal variables. Each Vσ,i→0V_{\sigma,i}\to0Vσ,i​→0 almost surely, although its mean remains one. For Tσ=∑i=1nVσ,iT_\sigma=\sum_{i=1}^nV_{\sigma,i}Tσ​=∑i=1n​Vσ,i​,

E∣Tσ−n∣=2n−2Emin⁡(Tσ,n),Emin⁡(Tσ,n)⟶0.\begin{aligned} &\mathbb E|T_\sigma-n|\\ &\quad=2n-2\mathbb E\min(T_\sigma,n),\\ &\mathbb E\min(T_\sigma,n)\longrightarrow0. \end{aligned}​E∣Tσ​−n∣=2n−2Emin(Tσ​,n),Emin(Tσ​,n)⟶0.​
(18)

The last line is bounded convergence. Therefore M(n)/M(1)→nM(n)/M(1)\to nM(n)/M(1)→n and κ1,n→1\kappa_{1,n}\to1κ1,n​→1. The order of limits matters. Every fixed lognormal law still has all power moments and belongs to the Gaussian domain of attraction.

A bounded numerical calculation¶

For nonnegative integrable sums, the exact lower-deviation identity is

M(n)=2E(nm−Sn)+.M(n)=2\mathbb E(nm-S_n)_+.M(n)=2E(nm−Sn​)+​.
(19)

For the mean-one lognormal, condition on the first n−1n-1n−1 summands and put a=n−∑i<nVσ,ia=n-\sum_{i<n}V_{\sigma,i}a=n−∑i<n​Vσ,i​. If a≤0a\le0a≤0, the conditional payoff is zero. For a>0a>0a>0, completing the square gives

h(a)=E(a−Vσ)+,d=log⁡(a)/σ+σ/2,h(a)=aΦ(d)−Φ(d−σ).\begin{aligned} h(a)&=\mathbb E(a-V_\sigma)_+,\\ d&=\log(a)/\sigma+\sigma/2,\\ h(a)&=a\Phi(d)-\Phi(d-\sigma). \end{aligned}h(a)dh(a)​=E(a−Vσ​)+​,=log(a)/σ+σ/2,=aΦ(d)−Φ(d−σ).​
(20)

The simulated payoff lies between zero and nnn. Multiplying its sample average by 2m2m2m estimates M(n)M(n)M(n) without estimating an unbounded upper-tail payoff. This uses a known model mean. It is not available merely because a dataset contains only small observations.

Use lognormal_sum_mad. The standard error below describes Monte Carlo integration, not uncertainty about the assumed lognormal law.

from xmath.incerto.concentration import lognormal_sum_mad, kappa_from_mads

for sigma in (0.5, 1, 2):
    single = lognormal_sum_mad(1, sigma)["mad"]
    result = lognormal_sum_mad(8, sigma, random_state=20261088)
    kappa = kappa_from_mads(single, result["mad"], 8)
    print(f"sigma={sigma:g}: MAD={result['mad']:.3f}, MC SE={result['mc_se']:.3f}, kappa={kappa:.3f}")

Output

sigma=1: MAD=4.413, MC SE=0.032, kappa=0.338
sigma=2: MAD=50.405, MC SE=0.254, kappa=0.707

Negative kappa needs no bimodality¶

Consider the symmetric triangular density f(x)=(2−∣x∣)/4f(x)=(2-|x|)/4f(x)=(2−∣x∣)/4 on [−2,2][-2,2][−2,2]. It has a single mode at zero and can be written as the sum of two independent Uniform[−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] variables. Direct integration gives M(1)=2/3M(1)=2/3M(1)=2/3. The sum of two copies is a sum of four such uniforms and has M(2)=14/15M(2)=14/15M(2)=14/15. Here is an explicit calculation of the second value. If TTT is a sum of four Uniform[0,1][0,1][0,1] variables, symmetry and integration of its CDF give

E∣2T−4∣=4∫02P(T<t) dt,P(T<t)=t4−4(t−1)+424,0≤t≤2,E∣2T−4∣=4(32−4)120=1415.\begin{aligned} \mathbb E|2T-4| &=4\int_0^2P(T<t)\,dt,\\ P(T<t)&=\frac{t^4-4(t-1)_+^4}{24},\\ &\hspace{2em}0\le t\le2,\\ \mathbb E|2T-4|&=\frac{4(32-4)}{120}=\frac{14}{15}. \end{aligned}E∣2T−4∣P(T<t)E∣2T−4∣​=4∫02​P(T<t)dt,=24t4−4(t−1)+4​​,0≤t≤2,=1204(32−4)​=1514​.​
(21)

The CDF formula is inclusion–exclusion for the volume below u1+⋯+u4<tu_1+\cdots+u_4<tu1​+⋯+u4​<t in the unit cube. Thus

κ1,2=2−log⁡2log⁡(7/5)<0.\kappa_{1,2}=2-\frac{\log2}{\log(7/5)}<0.κ1,2​=2−log(7/5)log2​<0.
(22)

This counterexample corrects the bimodality suggestion in §8.4.4, p. 162. Negative kappa says only that this MAD grows more slowly than the Gaussian benchmark across the chosen sizes.

The source’s separated Gaussian mixture is another example. For X=aR+σZX=aR+\sigma ZX=aR+σZ, with independent equiprobable R∈{−1,1}R\in\{-1,1\}R∈{−1,1} and standard-normal ZZZ, condition on the number KKK of positive signs:

K∼Binomial⁡(n,1/2),Sn∣K∼N(a(2K−n),nσ2).\begin{aligned} K&\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n,1/2),\\ S_n\mid K&\sim N(a(2K-n),n\sigma^2). \end{aligned}KSn​∣K​∼Binomial(n,1/2),∼N(a(2K−n),nσ2).​
(23)

If H(b,s)=E∣b+sZ∣H(b,s)=\mathbb E|b+sZ|H(b,s)=E∣b+sZ∣, splitting the normal integral at −b/s-b/s−b/s gives

H(b,s)=s2/π e−b2/(2s2)+∣b∣[2Φ(∣b∣/s)−1],M(n)=∑k=0n(nk)2−n×H(a(2k−n),σn).\begin{aligned} H(b,s)&=s\sqrt{2/\pi}\,e^{-b^2/(2s^2)}\\ &\quad+|b|[2\Phi(|b|/s)-1],\\ M(n)&=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom nk2^{-n}\\ &\quad\times H(a(2k-n),\sigma\sqrt n). \end{aligned}H(b,s)M(n)​=s2/π​e−b2/(2s2)+∣b∣[2Φ(∣b∣/s)−1],=k=0∑n​(kn​)2−n×H(a(2k−n),σn​).​
(24)

This finite mixture calculation underlies the figure. In particular, M(1)=H(a,σ)M(1)=H(a,\sigma)M(1)=H(a,σ) and M(2)={H(2a,2σ)+H(0,2σ)}/2M(2)=\{H(2a,\sqrt2\sigma)+H(0,\sqrt2\sigma)\}/2M(2)={H(2a,2​σ)+H(0,2​σ)}/2. For fixed σ>0\sigma>0σ>0 and a→∞a\to\inftya→∞, their ratio tends to one from above, so κ1,2→−∞\kappa_{1,2}\to-\inftyκ1,2​→−∞.

Use normal_location_mixture_sum_mad.

from xmath.incerto.concentration import normal_location_mixture_sum_mad, kappa_from_mads

for a in (0, 1, 3):
    m1 = normal_location_mixture_sum_mad(1, a)
    m2 = normal_location_mixture_sum_mad(2, a)
    print(f"separation={a:g}: kappa={kappa_from_mads(m1, m2, 2):.3f}")

Output

separation=0: kappa=0.000
separation=1: kappa=-0.134
separation=3: kappa=-2.028

Reproduce and continue¶

uv run python demos/incerto/concentration.py regenerates these figures and the sample-sufficiency figure. All curves are population calculations or explicitly labeled simulations. The sample-size calculation uses absolute error, not a universal threshold for confidence-interval validity.

Source locators: Taleb (2025), ch. 8, §§8.2–8.4, pp. 156–162, and §§8.6.1–8.6.4, pp. 164–169. The attached paper Taleb (2018) contains the earlier definition and derivations in §§II–IV and appendices D–G. The proofs, counterexample, computations and figures here are original treatments of that scope.
